titleAngles.myth: A pros and cons list is the rational way to make a big decision
titleAngles.book: The two-column list only weighs the options you already have; it never discovers option C
titleAngles.quote: It is an evaluation tool, not a discovery tool.

titleAngles.myth: When the whole room agrees fast, the team is aligned
titleAngles.book: Fast consensus buries hidden profiles; diverse rooms (Sommers's mock juries) think more accurately
titleAngles.quote: the only known antidote to this conformity trap is diversity

titleAngles.myth: Bad decisions go wrong at the moment we choose
titleAngles.book: They fail earlier, when the choice is framed as only two options - the city that filled in Collect Pond
titleAngles.quote: The failure happens in the framing.

description:
Charles Darwin, 29, rules a line down a notebook page: Marry on one side, Not Marry on the other. One of the greatest minds in history, reduced to a pros and cons list for the biggest choice of his life.

This is a Farsighted summary and analysis of Steven Johnson's book on how we make the decisions that matter most. The thesis: our worst life-changing decisions fail before we choose - at the moment we accept there are only two options. The tool that fixes it: widen the map before you choose.

We walk through the book's cases: the city that filled in Collect Pond instead of building Pierre L'Enfant's park (and got the Five Points slum), Franklin's moral algebra, the CIA's scale model of the Abbottabad compound, Meadow Lake's influence diagram, Samuel Sommers's mock juries, John Brennan's red team, Philip Tetlock's foxes and hedgehogs, Gary Klein's premortem, Johnson's own Brooklyn-or-California deadlock, and George Eliot's Middlemarch - plus an honest pushback on who actually has time for any of this.
